work.title: Products in daily use, not concepts in a deck.
work.lead: Every project starts with a clear operational problem. We build the solution and measure success through daily use.

nexora-control.summary: One dashboard for inventory, branch orders, and profit by SKU.
nexora-control.challenge: Warehouse, sales, and finance teams used three separate tools. Inventory and invoices rarely matched.
nexora-control.solution: One operational dashboard for real-time inventory, branch orders, and profit reporting by SKU.
nexora-control.result: Weekly reconciliation fell from two days to four hours.
nexora-control.body: Nexora ships goods to dozens of branches. Every morning, sales needs the same inventory figures the warehouse sees. We mapped the workflow from purchase order to invoice, then built one web application as the shared source of truth. Access is separated by role: warehouse staff record movements, sales checks availability, and finance downloads reports. We preserved how people work in the field while removing the wait for a weekend Excel file.

galleryAlt: Nexora Control — weekly sales performance chart
Nexora Control — operations team reviewing branch data

brightwork-people.summary: An HR portal for leave, payslips, and reviews across 500+ employees.
brightwork-people.challenge: Recruitment, attendance, and payroll were scattered across email and Excel for more than 500 employees.
brightwork-people.solution: A mobile-accessible HR portal for leave workflows, payslips, and performance reviews.
brightwork-people.result: New employee onboarding now takes two days instead of two weeks.
brightwork-people.body: BrightWork was growing quickly, but HR had become a bottleneck. We built a self-service employee portal for requesting leave, downloading payslips, and checking contract status. Managers receive an approval queue instead of another email folder. Existing employee data was integrated in stages so monthly payroll continued without disruption.
brightwork-people.imgAlt: BrightWork People — HR portal for leave, payslips, and reviews
galleryAlt: BrightWork People — HR meeting reviewing the onboarding flow

vela-atelier.summary: A branded store with loyalty and payments, connected to existing marketplaces.
vela-atelier.challenge: Online sales depended on marketplaces, leaving the brand without direct access to customer data.
vela-atelier.solution: A branded store with catalog, loyalty, and Midtrans payments, still connected to Shopee.
vela-atelier.result: Owned-channel revenue grew 2.4× in the first six months.
vela-atelier.body: Vela had a loyal customer base, but those customers shopped in someone else's storefront. We created a store that feels unmistakably theirs, with strong photography, clear sizing, and a short checkout. Inventory synchronization prevents overselling. The loyalty program brings repeat orders back to Vela's own channel instead of a marketplace algorithm.
vela-atelier.imgAlt: Vela Atelier — fashion storefront with catalog and loyalty program
galleryAlt: Vela Atelier — product details and branded shopping experience

paxia-table.summary: Live reservations for 12 outlets, QR menus, and POS synchronization.
paxia-table.challenge: Twelve outlets managed reservations through WhatsApp, causing double bookings almost every weekend.
paxia-table.solution: A live reservation system, QR menus, and POS synchronization for every outlet.
paxia-table.result: No-shows fell 35%, and weekend queues became predictable.
paxia-table.body: Paxia used to manage weekends through group chats. We replaced that process with a live table map for each outlet. Guests confirm through a link, hosts see remaining slots, and kitchens no longer guess cover counts. QR menus reduce printing and make branch-specific price updates simple.
paxia-table.imgAlt: Paxia Table — live reservations, QR menus, and restaurant table map
galleryAlt: Paxia Table — an outlet during weekend reservations

process.title: From brief to launch, with no guesswork.
process.lead: You see progress every week. Staging is always available. What we agree at the start is what we deliver at the end.
items: Listen first, propose second
We sit down with the founder or operations lead to understand who uses the product, where work gets stuck, and what must be live in the first week.
1–3 days
A plan you can rely on
Scope, architecture, wireframes, and timeline are documented. No surprise features appear halfway through without agreement.
3–5 days
Design ready for development
Screen flows, components, and a prototype let the business team click through the product before development begins.
5–10 days
Build in staging
You receive weekly updates and access to a test environment. Clients see the same product our engineers are building.
2–8 weeks
Test like a real user
We test function, speed, security, and presentation from mobile to desktop. Bugs are resolved before the domain moves.
3–7 days
Launch, then stay with you
We handle deployment, SSL, and monitoring, then support the first 30 days. Future features stay with the team that already knows the code.
Ongoing

faq.title: What should be clear from day one.
faq.lead: No withheld access, hidden fees, or code intentionally designed to keep you dependent on us.
faq.ownershipTitle: Your code, accounts, and access remain yours.
faq.ownershipCopy: We build products to hand over, not to lock clients into our services.
items: How long does a project take?

A business website typically takes 2–4 weeks. Web applications and operational systems usually take 4–10 weeks, depending on workflows, user roles, and integrations. We document the timeline and milestones before development begins, so you know what will be completed at every stage.
How many revision rounds are included?

Two major revision rounds during design are included. Feedback is consolidated by round to keep changes focused. We refine small changes in staging during development; requests that alter scope, workflows, or features are estimated and agreed together first.
Who owns the domain and hosting?

The client does. Domains, hosting or cloud accounts, analytics, email, and payment services are created in your company's name or transferred during handover. Lana Tech receives only the access required for setup and deployment; account ownership and billing remain with you.
Who owns the source code?

After the project is complete and paid in full, all custom source code, Git repositories, designs, content, and digital assets created specifically for the project belong entirely to the client. Open-source dependencies and third-party services retain their respective licenses without reducing your control over the product we build.
What is included at handover?

You receive the source-code repository, production and staging access, a list of required environment variables without secrets in documents, build and deployment instructions, and concise operational documentation. Another development team can continue the work without depending on Lana Tech accounts or identities.
Can our team or another vendor continue the work?

Yes. We use widely adopted technologies such as Next.js, Laravel, Node.js, and PostgreSQL—not closed platforms. Maintenance with Lana Tech is available as an option, never a requirement for the product to keep running.
Is the first consultation paid?

No. The initial meeting helps us understand the problem, users, and business goals. If there is a fit, we provide a scope, technical approach, timeline, and cost estimate you can evaluate without hidden commitments.
